criteria_results.title: Caption identifies correct case number

criteria_results.title: Caption identifies correct party names
criteria_results.reasoning: The caption correctly identifies Greenfield Botanical Sciences, Inc. as Plaintiff and Dr. Elena Vasquez and Canopy Ridge Therapeutics, LLC as Defendants.

criteria_results.title: Document includes a conclusion with prayer for relief

criteria_results.title: Addresses likelihood of success on the merits

criteria_results.title: Addresses irreparable harm factor
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly identifies irreparable harm as part of the preliminary injunction standard and includes a dedicated section, “III. GREENFIELD WILL SUFFER IRREPARABLE HARM ABSENT AN INJUNCTION,” analyzing why monetary damages are inadequate and why harm is imminent and difficult to quantify.

criteria_results.title: Addresses balance of hardships/equities factor
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly includes the balance of equities in the preliminary injunction standard and provides a dedicated section, “IV. THE BALANCE OF HARDSHIPS FAVORS GREENFIELD,” analyzing the relative harms to Greenfield, Dr. Vasquez, and Canopy Ridge.

criteria_results.title: Addresses public interest factor
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly includes the public interest as part of the preliminary injunction standard and provides a dedicated section titled “V. AN INJUNCTION SERVES THE PUBLIC INTEREST” analyzing why the requested injunction serves the public interest.

criteria_results.title: Identifies MNAA applicability
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly discusses the Massachusetts Noncompetition Agreement Act, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 149, § 24L, states that it applies to Dr. Vasquez’s non-compete, and analyzes multiple MNAA requirements including consideration, garden leave, duration, geography, scope, exemptions, and reformation.

criteria_results.title: Notes the agreement was entered into on or after October 1, 2018
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum states that Dr. Vasquez joined Greenfield on March 11, 2019 under an Employment Agreement containing the covenants, and expressly notes that because the covenant was entered into after October 1, 2018, the MNAA applies.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Addresses the 12-month general limitation on non-competes
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that the MNAA generally limits the restricted period to twelve months and then addresses the statutory exception permitting up to two years. It also identifies Dr. Vasquez’s covenant as a twenty-four-month restriction, thereby acknowledging that the contractual term exceeds the general 12-month limit.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Argues 24-month period enforceable via fiduciary duty exception
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum directly addresses the MNAA 12-month default and 24-month exception, arguing that the two-year restriction is enforceable because Dr. Vasquez both unlawfully took company property and independently breached fiduciary duties by copying trade secrets while employed and concealing it. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Addresses garden leave as MNAA consideration requirement
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly connects Section 7.3’s garden-leave clause—paying 50% of Dr. Vasquez’s base salary, identified elsewhere as $162,500/year or $13,541.67/month—to the MNAA’s consideration requirement, stating that it is the consideration required by Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 149, § 24L(b)(vii).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Identifies the 14,200 files / 3.8 GB USB download as misappropriation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly cites the forensic evidence that Dr. Vasquez copied approximately 14,200 files / 3.8 GB from restricted R&D directories to a personal SanDisk SSD during seven sessions from Dec. 1–12, 2024, and the trade-secret misappropriation argument characterizes that unauthorized copying to a personal device as acquisition by improper means and evidence of misappropriation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Identifies specific categories of trade secrets taken
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum specifically identifies all five listed categories of confidential information taken: the GBS-4400 formulation database, unpublished Phase II clinical trial data, proprietary SFE parameter sets, supplier list with pricing/exclusivity terms, and the five-year R&D roadmap.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Argues information qualifies as trade secrets — independent economic value
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly identifies independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable as a DTSA/MUTSA element and argues that the information is valuable because it is non-public, cannot be reverse-engineered, was developed through tens of millions in R&D investment, and was valued at $85 million with $52 million attributable to GBS-4400.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Argues Greenfield took reasonable measures to maintain secrecy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues the statutory reasonable-measures element, listing confidentiality agreements, role-based need-to-know access, MFA/VPN, encryption, file classification tags, key-card access, acceptable-use policies, exit audits, and Dr. Vasquez’s contractual acknowledgments.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: References Canopy Ridge press release language as circumstantial evidence
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum repeatedly ties Canopy Ridge’s February 24 press release language—describing CRT-7100 as derived from a rare Andean plant species using next-generation supercritical extraction—to the misappropriation theory, arguing that this description matches Greenfield’s GBS-4400 and is circumstantial evidence of use of the copied trade secrets.

criteria_results.title: Asserts trade secret misappropriation claim under DTSA
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly asserts trade secret misappropriation under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, citing 18 U.S.C. §§ 1836 and 1839, identifying DTSA elements, interstate-commerce nexus, misappropriation, and statutory injunctive relief.

criteria_results.title: Asserts trade secret misappropriation claim under Massachusetts Trade Secrets Act
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly asserts trade secret misappropriation under the Massachusetts Uniform Trade Secrets Act, citing Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93, §§ 42–42G and analyzing protectable trade secrets, misappropriation, and liability under that statute alongside the DTSA.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Does not assert a statutory presumption of irreparable harm under DTSA
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that Greenfield “does not rely on any presumption” and argues irreparable harm based on specific factual evidence, not on any DTSA statutory presumption. Although it notes that injunctions are authorized under the DTSA, it does not claim a presumption of irreparable harm.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Argues irreparable harm based on loss of trade secret protection
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues in the irreparable harm section that once Greenfield’s trade secrets are disclosed or absorbed by a competitor, their secrecy cannot be restored and no payment can make them “un-known.” It also argues loss of competitive head start and difficulty quantifying damages.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Argues money damages are inadequate
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues in the irreparable harm section that money damages are inadequate, emphasizing that secrecy cannot be restored once lost, Greenfield’s development head start/first-mover advantage would be eroded, future competitive harm is difficult to quantify, and valuation estimates exclude inherently unquantifiable harms such as investor confidence, financing, partnerships, and talent retention.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Uses specific financial facts to support irreparable harm
criteria_results.reasoning: The irreparable-harm section specifically cites Greenfield’s “$95 million estimate” and discusses it as a lower-bound sensitivity scenario for direct losses, thereby using a specific financial figure from the record to illustrate the magnitude and nature of harm.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Addresses garden leave payment in balance of hardships
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum's balance-of-hardships section expressly discusses the garden-leave payments as reducing Dr. Vasquez's hardship, stating that Greenfield offered her $162,500 per year to observe the covenant, that she returned the payment, and that she will receive garden-leave pay while subject to the restriction.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Addresses Dr. Vasquez's return of the garden leave payment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that Greenfield tendered the first garden-leave payment on February 1, 2025 and Dr. Vasquez returned it on February 5. It also addresses significance, arguing she cannot unilaterally void the non-compete by returning payments, that the agreement says return/refusal does not relieve obligations, and that Greenfield remains ready to tender payments as evidence of compliance/good faith.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Identifies Dr. Vasquez's solicitation of Dr. Lisa Chow
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that on February 20, 2025 Dr. Vasquez solicited Dr. Lisa Chow via a personal-account email, offered a senior role with at least a 40% pay increase, and uses this as direct evidence that she breached the non-solicitation covenant.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Uses solicitation as evidence of willingness to violate obligations
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum does more than mention the Chow solicitation as a standalone breach: it emphasizes that Dr. Vasquez solicited a former direct report through personal channels, requested secrecy, and that this showed she knew the conduct was forbidden. It also uses the solicitation to support irreparable harm and the need for an injunction to prevent further employee raiding, indicating she cannot be trusted to comply voluntarily.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Seeks injunctive relief enforcing the non-solicitation covenant
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum specifically requests enforcement of the non-solicitation covenant as injunctive relief, including a dedicated argument section on breach of the non-solicitation covenant and a requested injunction barring Dr. Vasquez from soliciting, recruiting, or hiring Greenfield employees through January 17, 2027.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Requests enforcement of non-compete against working at Canopy Ridge
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly requests preliminary injunctive relief enforcing the non-compete, including an order that Dr. Vasquez “shall not be employed by, or provide services to, Canopy Ridge” or similar competing plant-derived pharmaceutical entities within the restricted area through January 17, 2027.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Requests return or sequestration of misappropriated materials
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly requests return/neutral forensic sequestration of the allegedly exfiltrated materials, including delivery of the SanDisk SSD and all other devices, media, and accounts containing Greenfield data to a neutral forensic examiner for imaging, sequestration, and remediation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Requests forensic inspection of devices/systems
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly requests that Dr. Vasquez deliver the SanDisk SSD and that Defendants deliver all other devices, media, and accounts containing Greenfield data to a neutral forensic examiner, who will image, sequester, and remediate them under a court protocol. This satisfies the requirement for a forensic inspection/examination to identify and recover misappropriated trade secrets.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Relief is narrowly tailored — does not seek overbroad ban on all employment
criteria_results.reasoning: The requested injunction is limited to employment or services with Canopy Ridge or entities engaged in plant-derived pharmaceutical work within the 100-mile restricted territory, tied to the contractual non-compete and trade-secret concerns. The memorandum expressly notes Dr. Vasquez remains free to work outside the territory or outside plant-derived pharmaceuticals, so it does not seek to bar all employment of any kind.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Argues public interest in enforcing contracts and protecting trade secrets
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum’s public interest section expressly argues that the public interest favors enforcing freely negotiated contracts and protecting trade secrets, and that such protection encourages investment in innovation under the DTSA and MUTSA.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Acknowledges competing interest in employee mobility
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum acknowledges the employee-mobility/freedom-to-work interest in the balance-of-hardships discussion by recognizing that the injunction imposes a temporary employment restriction on Dr. Vasquez and arguing it is limited because she remains free to work outside the territory or outside plant-derived pharmaceuticals. Although it does not expressly frame this as a public-interest concern, it does mention the competing freedom-to-work interest.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Addresses or accounts for DTSA whistleblower notice deficiency
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum does not address the DTSA whistleblower immunity notice issue, but it also does not request DTSA exemplary damages or attorneys' fees; it seeks only preliminary injunctive and related equitable relief. Under the criterion, avoiding such a request satisfies the requirement.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Establishes subject matter jurisdiction
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum asserts DTSA and MUTSA claims and cites 18 U.S.C. § 1836, including the interstate-commerce nexus, but it does not address subject matter jurisdiction as such. It does not state that the Court has federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 based on the DTSA, supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 for state-law claims, or diversity jurisdiction.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Argues compressed timeline as evidence of pre-resignation negotiations
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum notes that Canopy Ridge announced Dr. Vasquez as CSO 38 days after her last day and separately cites pre-resignation visits to Canopy Ridge’s website, but it does not argue that the compressed 38-day hiring timeline is circumstantial evidence of pre-resignation negotiations with Canopy Ridge during or before the December 1–12 downloads.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Argues compressed timeline shows acceleration from trade secrets
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly links the compressed timing—Dr. Vasquez joining Canopy Ridge and the same-day announcement of an “accelerated” CRT-7100 Andean/SFE anti-inflammatory program—to her prior copying of Greenfield’s GBS-4400 trade-secret files. It argues this circumstantial timing suggests Canopy Ridge’s acceleration and “first to market” position derive from Greenfield’s misappropriated clinical/process data rather than independent development.

criteria_results.title: Anticipates and rebuts the defense that the non-compete is overbroad
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly anticipates an overbreadth/unenforceability challenge to the non-compete. It argues the 100-mile geographic scope is justified by Greenfield’s research operations and Dr. Vasquez’s responsibilities, notes Canopy Ridge is within the core restricted area, explains the activity restriction is limited to the plant-derived pharmaceutical field, and invokes the court’s authority under the MNAA and the agreement to reform or narrow the covenant if necessary.

criteria_results.title: Anticipates and rebuts the independent development defense
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum anticipates Canopy Ridge’s assertion that CRT-7100 was independently developed and rebuts it with circumstantial evidence, including Dr. Vasquez’s exfiltration timeline, her rapid hiring as CSO, Canopy Ridge’s simultaneous announcement of an accelerated Andean/SFE anti-inflammatory program resembling GBS-4400, and its prior lack of disclosure of such a program. It also notes that if CRT-7100 were truly independent, an injunction barring use of Greenfield data would impose no burden.

criteria_results.title: Anticipates and rebuts the defense that 24-month restriction is unreasonable
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum directly addresses the 24-month duration under the MNAA, acknowledges the general 12-month limit, and rebuts unreasonableness by invoking the statutory exception allowing up to two years where the employee breached fiduciary duties or unlawfully took employer property. It applies both exceptions to Dr. Vasquez’s alleged conduct and also requests enforcement on narrower terms if necessary.

criteria_results.title: Anticipates and rebuts defense that no actual use of trade secrets occurred
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum directly addresses the likely defense that there has been no actual use or disclosure, stating that use may be proven by circumstantial evidence. It rebuts the defense with evidence of the file downloads, concealment, Dr. Vasquez’s move to a direct competitor, Canopy Ridge’s strikingly similar Andean/SFE anti-inflammatory CRT-7100, its accelerated timeline/first-to-market statements, and the practical inevitability that she would draw on the taken GBS-4400 data in her CSO role.

criteria_results.title: Addresses breach of non-compete as a likelihood-of-success claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum includes a likelihood-of-success section on contract claims addressing the non-compete, explaining enforceability under the MNAA and facts showing breach: Dr. Vasquez joined Canopy Ridge as CSO within weeks of separation, Canopy Ridge is a competitor in plant-derived pharmaceuticals, and its Waltham headquarters is within the 100-mile restricted territory during the 24-month restricted period.

criteria_results.title: Addresses breach of confidentiality covenant as a likelihood-of-success claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum includes a likelihood-of-success section for contract claims and expressly argues that Dr. Vasquez breached her confidentiality covenants, citing the forensic evidence of unauthorized USB transfers/personal email forwarding and potential use/disclosure of confidential information. Although it references Sections 8.1/8.2 somewhat inconsistently, it addresses the confidentiality covenant breach as a likelihood-of-success claim.

criteria_results.title: References the $47.3 million R&D investment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that Greenfield has invested about $47.3 million in R&D since 2016 and later repeats the $47.3 million investment figure.

criteria_results.title: References GBS-4400 as the lead compound in Phase II trials
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly states that Greenfield's lead compound is GBS-4400 and that it is in FDA Phase II trials.

criteria_results.title: References the Linden Valuation Group trade secret valuation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly references the independent Linden Valuation Group valuation, stating that LVG valued the portfolio at $85 million, with $52 million attributable to GBS-4400, and cites the LVG report in several sections.

criteria_results.title: References CRT-7100 as Canopy Ridge's competing compound
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum repeatedly mentions CRT-7100, identifying it as Canopy Ridge's accelerated lead anti-inflammatory derived from a rare/high-altitude Andean plant species and using supercritical extraction, in competition with Greenfield's GBS-4400.

criteria_results.title: References the January 28, 2025 cease-and-desist letter
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that on January 28, 2025, Greenfield’s counsel demanded return/certification and covenant compliance, and that Dr. Vasquez acknowledged receipt but did not respond substantively.

criteria_results.title: Cites applicable case law in support of arguments
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum cites numerous case law authorities supporting the PI standard and substantive arguments, including Winter, Arborjet, New Comm Wireless, Ross-Simons, Jet Spray Cooler, Incase, Boulanger, Marine Contractors, Chelsea Industries, Augat, Corporate Technologies, K-Mart, and Crowley. This exceeds the minimum of three cases.

criteria_results.title: References Dr. Vasquez's role and unique access to trade secrets
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum identifies Dr. Vasquez as Vice President of Research, states that she led the GBS-4400 program, and explains her unusually broad access to Greenfield’s most sensitive trade secrets, including being one of only seven with access to the formulation database and one of four with access to the full SFE repository. It also links her senior role and competitor employment to heightened harm.

criteria_results.title: References the timing of file downloads relative to resignation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly states that Dr. Vasquez copied approximately 14,200 files in seven sessions from December 1–12, 2024, resigned on December 12, 2024, and that the final copy session ended that evening, thereby highlighting the temporal connection to her departure.
